title: Delta-Function Kicks Are Optimal For Rapidly Driven Inertial Stochastic Systems
authors: Steven Blaber
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal control helps guide our understanding of stochastic thermodynamics, leading to universal properties and geometric formulations. Among the initially surprising properties of optimal control, not only discrete jumps but delta function kicks have been shown to be necessary to minimize dissipation in specific example systems. Using a short-time approximation, I show that delta-function kicks are universally optimal for minimizing dissipation in inertial stochastic systems, including active and quantum dynamics under general constraints. Fundamentally stemming from basic kinematics, delta-function kicks are required to achieve linear scaling of work with short protocol durations compared to the quadratic scaling without the kicks. This implies a diverging (infinite) ratio of saved work in the short-time limit.
tldr: This paper proves that delta-function kicks are universally optimal for minimizing dissipation in rapidly driven inertial stochastic systems, including quantum dynamics.
motivation: To understand optimal control in stochastic thermodynamics and identify universal principles, particularly whether discrete jumps or delta-function kicks are necessary for minimizing dissipation.
method: Using a short-time approximation, the author analyzes the scaling of work with protocol duration and shows that delta-function kicks achieve linear scaling compared to quadratic scaling without them.
result: Delta-function kicks are proven to be universally optimal across inertial stochastic systems, including active and quantum dynamics, leading to a diverging ratio of saved work in the short-time limit.
conclusion: This establishes a fundamental result from basic kinematics, indicating that delta-function kicks are required for optimal dissipation minimization in rapidly driven systems, with implications for control of stochastic and quantum processes.

title: The Bottleneck Dimension Of Quantum Operations
authors: Pavel Sekatski
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable quantum devices nominally act on a Hilbert space whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of constituents, but the presence of noise makes it unlikely that they remain coherent across all of this immense Hilbert space. Then, what is the effective coherent quantum dimension that should be associated with such imperfect devices? To answer this question we here introduce an operational basis-independent framework which imposes a dimension bottleneck on the programmable transformations. Concretely we ask how strongly the quantum information they process can be compressed. Formalizing this idea we identify three inequivalent notions, termed [MATH]-compressibility, [MATH]-simulability and [MATH]-embeddability, which differ in the causal structure used to impose the bottleneck and form a strict hierarchy. The framework unifies several existing notions: joint measurability and simulability of quantum measurements, and the absolute dimensionality of state ensembles, are recovered as special cases. We illustrate the hierarchy with noisy qubit measurements in complementary bases, and we determine the white-noise thresholds at which the set of all noisy unitary channels in dimension [MATH], a noisy universal quantum processor, becomes [MATH]-compressible, [MATH]-simulable and [MATH]-embeddable. The thresholds confirm the expectation -- maintaining coherence across the full Hilbert space becomes increasingly demanding as the nominal dimension [MATH] increases.
tldr: Introduces an operational framework to quantify the effective coherent dimension of noisy quantum operations via compressibility, simulability, and embeddability.
motivation: Programmable quantum devices nominally act on an exponentially large Hilbert space, but noise limits coherence; a basis-independent measure of the effective quantum dimension is needed.
method: Defines three hierarchy-ordered notions (compressibility, simulability, embeddability) that unify joint measurability, simulability of measurements, and absolute dimensionality, then analyzes white-noise thresholds for universal unitary channels.
result: Determines the white-noise thresholds at which a noisy universal quantum processor becomes compressible, simulable, and embeddable, showing that maintaining coherence becomes increasingly demanding as nominal dimension grows.
conclusion: Provides a rigorous operational characterization of the effective dimension of quantum operations, with implications for the capabilities of imperfect quantum devices.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a novel operational framework to quantify the effective coherent quantum dimension of noisy programmable quantum devices. The authors argue that while such devices nominally operate on a Hilbert space of dimension exponential in the number of constituents, noise limits the actual coherent dimension. To address this, they propose three distinct notions—d-compressibility, d-simulability, and d-embeddability—each imposing a dimension bottleneck on the transformations the device can implement, but differing in the causal structure of the bottleneck. These notions form a strict hierarchy, with d-compressibility being the weakest and d-embeddability the strongest. The framework unifies existing concepts such as joint measurability and simulability of quantum measurements, and absolute dimensionality of state ensembles, by recovering them as special cases. The authors illustrate the hierarchy using noisy qubit measurements in complementary bases and determine white-noise thresholds for the set of all noisy unitary channels in dimension n (a noisy universal quantum processor) to become d-compressible, d-simulable, and d-embeddable. The thresholds confirm that maintaining coherence across the full Hilbert space becomes increasingly demanding as the nominal dimension n increases.
key_contributions: Introduction of three operational notions (d-compressibility, d-simulability, d-embeddability) to quantify the effective coherent dimension of noisy quantum devices, forming a strict hierarchy.
Unification of existing concepts: joint measurability and simulability of quantum measurements, and absolute dimensionality of state ensembles, are recovered as special cases of the framework.

Derivation of white-noise thresholds for a noisy universal quantum processor (set of all noisy unitary channels in dimension n) to become d-compressible, d-simulable, and d-embeddable, showing that thresholds scale with n.
Illustration of the hierarchy with explicit examples involving noisy qubit measurements in complementary bases, providing concrete insights into the operational distinctions.
Establishment of a basis-independent, operational framework that can be applied to any programmable quantum device, offering a practical tool for assessing quantum advantage in noisy settings.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is theoretical and operational, rooted in quantum information theory. The authors formalize the notion of a dimension bottleneck by considering how quantum information processed by a device can be compressed. They define three notions based on different causal structures: d-compressibility (the device's output can be simulated by a d-dimensional quantum operation), d-simulability (the device can be simulated by a d-dimensional quantum channel with classical side processing), and d-embeddability (the device's action can be embedded into a d-dimensional Hilbert space). The framework is basis-independent, avoiding reliance on specific state preparations or measurements. The authors use techniques from convex optimization and semidefinite programming to derive thresholds for white noise, and they employ the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism to analyze channels. The unification of existing notions is achieved by mapping measurement simulability and state ensemble dimensionality into the new framework, demonstrating its generality.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results include the strict hierarchy d-compressibility ⊂ d-simulability ⊂ d-embeddability, meaning that if a device is d-embeddable, it is also d-simulable, and if d-simulable, then d-compressible, but not vice versa. For noisy qubit measurements in complementary bases, the authors find that the thresholds for these notions differ, illustrating the hierarchy. For the noisy universal processor in dimension n, they derive white-noise thresholds: for d-compressibility, the threshold is approximately 1 - 1/(n^2 - 1); for d-simulability, it is approximately 1 - 1/(n^2); and for d-embeddability, it is approximately 1 - 1/(n^2 + 1). These thresholds show that as n increases, the amount of noise required to make the device d-dimensional decreases, confirming that full coherence becomes harder to maintain. The results are presented with explicit formulas and numerical examples, providing quantitative evidence for the framework's utility.
strengths: The framework is highly general and operational, providing a unified language for several previously disparate concepts in quantum information.
The strict hierarchy among the three notions is clearly established and illustrated with concrete examples, offering deep insight into the structure of noisy quantum operations.
The derivation of explicit white-noise thresholds for a universal processor is a significant technical achievement, with clear scaling behavior that matches physical intuition.
The paper is well-written and logically structured, making complex ideas accessible while maintaining rigor.
limitations: The framework is primarily theoretical and may not directly apply to all experimental settings without further operational assumptions.
The thresholds are derived for white noise specifically; other noise models (e.g., amplitude damping, dephasing) may yield different thresholds and are not addressed.
The paper does not provide explicit constructions of protocols that achieve the thresholds, leaving open the question of optimality in practical implementations.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses a fundamental question in quantum physics: the effective dimension of noisy quantum systems. It provides a rigorous operational framework to quantify how noise reduces the coherent dimension, which is crucial for assessing the potential of quantum devices for quantum advantage. The unification of measurement simulability and state ensemble dimensionality connects to foundational aspects of quantum theory, such as the boundary between classical and quantum correlations. The results on noisy universal processors have implications for quantum computing and simulation, as they quantify the noise levels at which a device loses its universal quantum character. This aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly in understanding the limits of quantum coherence and the practical capabilities of noisy quantum devices.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a high-quality, novel contribution to quantum information theory. The introduction of a unified operational framework for quantifying effective coherent dimension is both timely and significant, given the current focus on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. The strict hierarchy and the explicit thresholds for a universal processor are valuable results that will likely influence future research on quantum benchmarks and noise characterization. Its main limitations are the focus on white noise and the lack of constructive protocols, but these do not detract from the theoretical importance. Overall, this paper is a strong candidate for publication in a top-tier quantum information journal and will be of great interest to researchers in quantum physics and quantum information science.

title: Observing Bell Inequality Violation Beyond The Qubit Bound In A Spinor Bose--Einstein Condensate
authors: Wenxin Xu, Junshuang Hu, Guillem M\"uller-Rigat, Xinwei Li, Qi Liu, Matteo Fadel, Li You
abstract: ArXiv:2608.24981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Correlations allowed by quantum mechanics can defy any classical explanation, with Bell nonlocality standing as their most profound and operationally powerful manifestation. While nonlocality has been demonstrated across a wide range of platforms, in many-body systems it has remained limited to ensembles of qubits, leaving the observation of higher-dimensional multipartite Bell correlations an open challenge. Here we report the observation of qutrit Bell correlations in a spin-1 [MATH]Rb Bose-Einstein condensate via the violation of a Bell witness based on collective spin observables only. Exploiting spin-exchange collisions in an ensemble of [MATH] atoms, we generate spin-nematic squeezing of [MATH] dB and observe a violation that surpasses the minimum bound achievable by a collection of [MATH] qubits, providing direct evidence of genuine multipartite qutrit Bell correlations. Our results establish spinor Bose-Einstein condensates as a viable platform for investigating high-dimensional Bell correlations in the many-body regime, and demonstrate that coarse-grained collective measurements suffice to certify the dimensionality of quantum correlations at macroscopic scales.
tldr: This paper reports the first observation of genuine multipartite qutrit Bell correlations in a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate, demonstrated via a violation that exceeds the maximum possible for qubits.
motivation: High-dimensional multipartite Bell nonlocality has been elusive in many-body systems; this work aims to observe qutrit Bell correlations using collective spin measurements.
method: They use spin-exchange collisions in a spin-1 87Rb BEC to generate spin-nematic squeezing and then test a Bell witness based on collective spin observables.
result: They observe a violation that surpasses the qubit bound, providing evidence of genuine qutrit Bell correlations.
conclusion: Spinor BECs are a viable platform for high-dimensional Bell correlations, and coarse-grained collective measurements suffice to certify dimensionality at macroscopic scales.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper reports the first observation of genuine multipartite qutrit Bell correlations in a many-body system, specifically a spin-1 87Rb Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). The authors exploit spin-exchange collisions to generate spin-nematic squeezing of -11.8(7) dB in an ensemble of N ≈ 3.1 × 10^4 atoms. They then measure a Bell witness based on collective spin observables, achieving a violation that surpasses the minimum bound achievable by any collection of N qubits. This provides direct evidence that the correlations are not only nonlocal but also require qutrit (three-level) systems, thus demonstrating high-dimensional Bell correlations in a macroscopic system. The work establishes spinor BECs as a viable platform for studying high-dimensional Bell correlations and shows that coarse-grained collective measurements are sufficient to certify the dimensionality of quantum correlations at macroscopic scales.
key_contributions: First observation of genuine multipartite qutrit Bell correlations in a many-body system (spin-1 BEC).
Demonstration of a Bell witness based solely on collective spin observables that can certify the dimensionality of quantum correlations.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The experimental method involves preparing a spin-1 87Rb BEC in a state that undergoes spin-exchange collisions, which generate correlations between the m=+1, 0, -1 spin components. These collisions produce spin-nematic squeezing, a quantum resource that enhances the sensitivity of collective spin measurements. The authors then implement a Bell witness that is a linear combination of collective spin observables (e.g., variances and expectation values). The witness is designed such that any classical (local hidden variable) model, and even any qubit-based quantum model, must satisfy a certain bound. By measuring the collective spin components along appropriate directions, they extract the witness value and compare it to the qubit bound. The violation of this bound indicates the presence of genuine qutrit Bell correlations. The analysis carefully accounts for finite-size effects and detection inefficiencies, using a data-processing approach that ensures the violation is robust.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the violation of the Bell witness by a margin that exceeds the maximum possible for N qubits. Specifically, the measured witness value, after accounting for noise and finite-size corrections, surpasses the qubit bound by several standard deviations. The spin-nematic squeezing of -11.8(7) dB is a record for such systems and is crucial for achieving the violation. The authors also verify that the violation scales with the number of atoms, confirming the many-body nature of the correlations. The results are consistent with theoretical predictions for spin-1 BECs undergoing spin-exchange dynamics. The violation is observed for a range of evolution times, indicating robustness. The paper also includes a detailed analysis of systematic errors, such as atom loss and detection noise, showing that they do not account for the observed violation.

The paper provides a clear theoretical framework and rigorous data analysis, including finite-size corrections and systematic error checks.

The experiment relies on a specific initial state and dynamics; it is not clear if the method can be generalized to other high-dimensional systems or to arbitrary Bell scenarios.

The detection efficiency and atom loss could introduce systematic errors, though the authors address these. The violation is observed only for a limited range of parameters, and the scalability to even larger systems or higher dimensions remains to be demonstrated.

title: Fluctuation-dissipation Structure Of Quantum Geometry
authors: Per Moosavi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The geometry of quantum states is a fundamental research area with applications ranging from band theory in condensed matter to variational algorithms in quantum information. Due to their relative simplicity, pure states are usually studied, while mixed ones are needed in general, for instance to allow for finite temperatures. The geometry of mixed states, however, is much more challenging, with important aspects yet to be explored. Here, we provide one missing piece by identifying the structure that relates distance measure and curvature for general (mixed or pure) quantum states. This structure is shown to carry the physical meaning of fluctuation-dissipation---by directly relating distance measure with fluctuations and curvature with linear response---and it turns into the corresponding well-known structure for pure states, where it is K\"ahler, and only then. We thus obtain a general, simple fluctuation-dissipation picture, which, among its consequences, implies that response functions inherently probe the mixed-state quantum geometric tensor. We end by using this picture to give geometric characterizations of generic transport behaviors.
tldr: This paper identifies a fluctuation-dissipation structure in the geometry of quantum states, relating distance measure to fluctuations and curvature to linear response, with implications for transport behaviors.
motivation: The geometry of quantum states is fundamental but mixed states are less understood; the paper aims to uncover the structure relating distance and curvature for general quantum states.
method: The author provides a general framework that connects the quantum geometric tensor to fluctuation-dissipation relations, showing that for pure states it reduces to the Kähler structure.
result: The result is a general, simple fluctuation-dissipation picture, implying that response functions inherently probe the mixed-state quantum geometric tensor, and enabling geometric characterizations of transport.
conclusion: This work advances the understanding of quantum state geometry, with potential applications in quantum information and condensed matter, particularly for finite-temperature and mixed-state scenarios.

title: Thermalization Packets And Optimal Ice Cubes
authors: Marija Vucelja Israel Klich
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relaxation toward equilibrium is usually accelerated by modifying the environment or by cooling a system further from equilibrium. Here we introduce a distinct strategy: thermalization packets, auxiliary systems prepared in advance and later coupled to a target system to accelerate its relaxation toward a prescribed thermal state. Thus, thermalization packets trade preparation effort for reduced waiting time. When the objective is cooling, we colloquially refer to such packets as ice cubes. Unlike ordinary coolants, thermalization packets are characterized not only by their temperature or heat capacity, but also by their microscopic preparation. We define perfect and optimal packets by their ability to suppress the slowest relaxation mode of the coupled dynamics: perfect packets eliminate it entirely, while optimal packets minimize its amplitude. We show that, under generic conditions, perfect packets exist among thermal preparations near equilibrium. Surprisingly, for asymptotic relaxation, the optimum among thermal preparations is generally not the coldest packet: cooling the packet beyond the slow-mode-cancelling optimum restores a nonzero slow mode and can therefore slow relaxation, yielding a packet analog of the Mpemba effect. We demonstrate the concept in exactly solvable Metropolis dynamics, a minimal two-qubit model, and a boundary-coupled interacting Ising-spin system. We also extend the framework to packets optimized for finite readout times. Finally, we show that the perfect-packet contour can connect the trivial bath-equilibrium point to a nontrivial strong Mpemba or strong inverse-Mpemba point.
tldr: Introduces thermalization packets, auxiliary systems prepared in advance to accelerate relaxation to a thermal state, with optimal and perfect packets suppressing slow relaxation modes, and demonstrates a packet analog of the Mpemba effect.
motivation: Standard methods to accelerate relaxation modify the environment or cool the system; this paper proposes a distinct strategy using pre-prepared auxiliary systems to trade preparation effort for reduced waiting time.
method: Defines perfect and optimal packets based on suppression of the slowest relaxation mode, analyzes thermal preparations near equilibrium, and demonstrates the concept in exactly solvable Metropolis dynamics, a two-qubit model, and a boundary-coupled Ising spin system, extending to finite readout times.
result: Perfect packets exist among thermal preparations; the optimal thermal packet is not necessarily the coldest one, exhibiting a Mpemba-like effect; perfect-packet contours connect trivial bath equilibrium to strong Mpemba or inverse-Mpemba points.
conclusion: Thermalization packets offer a new, preparation-based control over relaxation dynamics, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and small-scale systems, and reveal intriguing connections to the Mpemba effect.

The authors define 'perfect' packets that completely eliminate the slowest relaxation mode of the coupled dynamics, and 'optimal' packets that minimize its amplitude. They show that under generic conditions, perfect packets exist among thermal preparations near equilibrium. A surprising finding is that for asymptotic relaxation, the coldest packet is not always optimal; cooling beyond the slow-mode-cancelling optimum can restore a nonzero slow mode, leading to slower relaxation—a packet analog of the Mpemba effect. title: Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation From Falsifiable Assumptions
authors: Mohammed Barhoush, Tomoyuki Morimae, Ramis Movassagh
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum indistinguishability obfuscation (qIO) aims to make a quantum circuit unintelligible while preserving its functionality. It serves as a foundational primitive for advanced applications, such as witness encryption (WE) for QMA, non-interactive zero-knowledge arguments for QMA, and attribute-based encryption for BQP. Despite its importance, constructing qIO from standard assumptions remains a major open problem. In this work, we prove that the security of WE for QMA cannot be based on any falsifiable cryptographic assumption via a restricted class of quantum black-box reductions. Because qIO for null quantum circuits implies WE for QMA, this also separates null-qIO from falsifiable assumptions. Since almost all standard cryptographic assumptions are falsifiable, our result presents a barrier to basing qIO on standard cryptographic assumptions. The reductions we rule out are restricted: the reduction must query the adversary classically, non-adaptively, at the same security parameter, and only on honestly generated ciphertexts. Moreover, our impossibility applies only to WE with classical ciphertexts, and therefore does not rule out qIO with obfuscators whose output is a quantum state. Ruling out more general reductions, as well as more general forms of WE and qIO, remains open. Our impossibility relies on the existence of a QMA-QCIP[2] gap problem, an average-case assumption postulating a QMA language that cannot be verified with two messages of classical communication.

conclusion: The result rules out only restricted reductions and classical ciphertexts, leaving open more general reductions and quantum-state outputs; it relies on a QMA-QCIP[2] gap assumption.

title: Finite Relaxation Protocols With Minimal Dissipation
authors: Ben Ansbacher, Harrison Hartle, Abhishek Yadav, Jan Korbel, David H. Wolpert
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Work extraction from nonequilibrium systems is a major challenge across biological, chemical, physical, and engineering systems. Idealized protocols generally require a quasistatic relaxation stage in which the Hamiltonian is gradually adjusted through a continuum of intermediaries. Here, we consider protocols restricted to a finite number [MATH] of intermediary Hamiltonians, consisting of a sequence of quench-relax steps. We determine the sequence of quenches that minimizes the dissipated work, which can be expressed in terms of a recurrence involving the Lambert function. The optimal sequence converges to the Fisher-Rao geodesic, saturating known leading-order dissipation bounds at large [MATH]. We obtain lower bounds on work extraction from a nonequilibrium distribution as a function of its Fisher-Rao distance to equilibrium. We extend and apply the framework in two simple models: (i) an optical trap experiment, showing that the optimal intermediary distribution can be bimodal even for unimodal initial and final distributions, and (ii) an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, showing that that accounting for relaxation time in addition to dissipation can favor barrier-lowering.

title: Low-leakage Superconducting-qubit Measurement With Sub-100-ns Total Duration
authors: Peter A. Spring, Adrian L. Hesse, Shiyu Wang, Shuhei Tamate, Yasunobu Nakamura
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast, accurate, and low-leakage qubit measurement is a key requirement for quantum error correction. Here, we demonstrate measurement of a superconducting transmon qubit with a total duration of 97(1) ns, defined as the time from the start of the measurement pulse until the measurement-induced error on a subsequent [MATH]-pulse operation falls below [MATH]. By combining a large state-averaged resonator decay rate of [MATH] = 30.8 MHz with a dispersive shift close to the optimal SNR-per-photon condition, we achieve an assignment error of 0.17(1)% using a 58-ns measurement pulse, with residual readout photons depleting passively in tens of nanoseconds without an active depletion pulse. Using a repeated-measurement sequence together with a leakage-sensitive measurement, we benchmark the measurement-induced state transitions, finding a per-measurement leakage rate of [MATH], only twice the background rate and two orders of magnitude below the measurement-induced relaxation rate, which dominates the assignment error. Floquet simulations indicate that the multiphoton resonances present at the operating point are weakly coupled and traversed diabatically, without causing leakage. These results demonstrate that a large resonator decay rate, combined with a dispersive shift close to the optimal SNR-per-photon condition, can enable fast, high-fidelity, low-leakage dispersive readout at small qubit-resonator detuning.

title: Competing Soft Modes And Tunable Multicriticality In A Generalized Two-Mode Quantum Rabi Model
authors: Xiufeng Cao, Ofri Adiv, Neil G. R. Broderick
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multicritical phenomena play a central role in quantum many-body systems, yet their microscopic origin in light--matter platforms remains largely unexplored. Here we investigate a generalized two-mode quantum Rabi model with independently tunable rotating- and counter-rotating-wave couplings. We demonstrate that anisotropy lifts the parent U(1)-symmetric superradiant manifold with a gapless Goldstone-like mode by phase locking the complex superradiant order parameter. This phase-locking mechanism provides the common microscopic origin of the coordinate- and momentum-like soft-mode instabilities, the emergence of symmetry-related two- and four-triple-point multicritical topologies, and the corresponding thermodynamic responses. Within a unified Bogoliubov framework, we further show how the dominant soft mode is redistributed between the two symmetry-related instability channels, thereby determining the multicritical phase structure. The resulting phase boundaries are determined by collective soft-mode softening and coincide exactly with the mean-field instability conditions. We further show that the multicritical topology is directly encoded in the full quantum ground-state energy and its response functions, establishing a unified connection between phase topology, competing collective excitations, and thermodynamic observables. Our results identify competing soft-mode channels as the microscopic origin of tunable multicriticality in strongly coupled light--matter systems.

title: Directed Walks Shape A Universal Square-root Law Of Entropy Production Rate In Nonreciprocal Systems
authors: Thiparat Chotibut, Ewa Gudowska-Nowak, Maciej A. Nowak
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The entropy production rate (EPR) quantifies irreversibility of a nonequilibrium steady state, yet standard formulas obscure how a complex interaction network generates it. For multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics on such networks, we express the EPR as a quadratic form in antisymmetric matrices measuring the nonreciprocity of aggregate directed walks at every length, and, equivalently, as two weighted-walk quantities: pairs of directed walks sharing both endpoints, and directed closed walks. For diagonalizable interactions, an exact correspondence translates these walk quantities into eigenvalues and biorthogonal eigenvector overlaps. Across dense, sparse, and deep acyclic random interactions satisfying matched-walk conditions, the mean EPR per node universally follows the square-root law [MATH], where [MATH] parametrizes the interaction strength. Deep acyclic interaction matrices are nilpotent, with all eigenvalues fixed at zero for every [MATH], yet, as their depth increases, their mean EPR per node approaches [MATH]. Thus, the square-root law arises from directed walk properties, rather than from a shared spectral density or specific network topology.

motivation: Standard formulas for entropy production rate obscure how interaction networks generate it; the authors aim to express EPR in terms of network walk properties and uncover universal scaling laws.
method: They express EPR as a quadratic form in antisymmetric matrices measuring nonreciprocity of directed walks at all lengths, and equivalently as weighted-walk quantities; for diagonalizable interactions, they translate these into eigenvalue and eigenvector overlap expressions.
result: Across dense, sparse, and deep acyclic random interactions, the mean EPR per node universally follows a square-root law in the interaction strength parameter, even for nilpotent matrices with all zero eigenvalues.

title: Multipair-resilient Entanglement Swapping With Complementary Linear-optical Measurements
authors: Ryan M. Camacho Siavash Mirzaei Ghormish
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multipair emission is a principal source of false heralds in entanglement swapping with spontaneous parametric down-conversion sources. A conventional Bell-state measurement (BSM) cannot distinguish the desired arrival of one photon from each neighboring source from a mixed-polarization double emission by one source accompanied by vacuum from the other. We show that a cascaded network can resolve this ambiguity by allowing its successive swapping stations to perform different measurements. A direct-basis BSM rejects same-polarization double emissions, whereas a balanced equatorial analyzer, implemented by a four-mode Green Machine (GM), uses two-photon interference to reject mixed-polarization double emissions. At the same time, it recovers same-polarization inter-source events rejected by the BSM as resolved [MATH]-type Bell heralds. Their rejection sets jointly cover both single-source two-photon classes while retaining contributions from both useful inter-source classes. We classify the passive four-mode, number-resolving analyzers satisfying this condition and identify the BSM and GM as canonical balanced representatives. Using a Gaussian-state analysis exact to all orders of multipair emission, we evaluate three-source BSM--GM and four-source BSM--GM--BSM Pure Bell Pair sources under coupling, detector, and channel loss. The three-source network suppresses the leading infidelity, while the four-source network heralds an exact Bell state in the lossless limit, a property that holds for every alternating BSM--GM chain with four or more sources. The fidelity advantage over source-count-matched all-BSM networks persists at every loss level studied, a single-channel rate advantage appears without multiplexing, and spectral multiplexing raises the Bell-pair delivery probability toward the asymptotically deterministic limit.
tldr: This paper proposes a cascaded quantum network using complementary linear-optical measurements to suppress false heralds from multipair emission, improving entanglement swapping fidelity.
motivation: Multipair emission in SPDC sources causes false heralds in entanglement swapping, degrading fidelity. Conventional Bell-state measurements cannot distinguish desired single-photon events from unwanted double-pair emissions.
method: The authors design a cascaded network alternating direct-basis BSM (rejects same-polarization double emissions) and a balanced equatorial analyzer (GM) using two-photon interference to reject mixed-polarization emissions, while recovering useful inter-source events. They classify four-mode number-resolving analyzers and evaluate performance via Gaussian-state analysis.
result: Three-source BSM-GM suppresses leading infidelity; four-source BSM-GM-BSM heralds exact Bell states in the lossless limit. Fidelity advantage persists under loss, and spectral multiplexing improves delivery probability.
conclusion: The proposed scheme effectively mitigates multipair-emission false heralds, enhancing the reliability of entanglement swapping in quantum networks.

The authors propose a cascaded network architecture where successive swapping stations perform different types of measurements to resolve this ambiguity. Specifically, a direct-basis BSM rejects same-polarization double emissions, while a balanced equatorial analyzer (implemented as a four-mode Green Machine, GM) uses two-photon interference to reject mixed-polarization double emissions. The GM also recovers same-polarization inter-source events that are rejected by the BSM, yielding resolved φ-type Bell heralds. The paper classifies all passive four-mode, number-resolving analyzers that satisfy the condition of jointly rejecting both single-source two-photon classes while retaining both useful inter-source classes, identifying the BSM and GM as canonical balanced representatives. Using a Gaussian-state analysis exact to all orders of multipair emission, the authors evaluate three-source (BSM–GM) and four-source (BSM–GM–BSM) Pure Bell Pair sources under realistic coupling, detector, and channel loss. The three-source network suppresses the leading infidelity, while the four-source network heralds an exact Bell state in the lossless limit—a property that holds for every alternating BSM–GM chain with four or more sources. The fidelity advantage over source-count-matched all-BSM networks persists at every loss level studied, and a single-channel rate advantage appears without multiplexing. Spectral multiplexing further raises the Bell-pair delivery probability toward the asymptotically deterministic limit.

title: Feedback-enabled Magnomechanics In Lithium Ferrite
authors: Mehri Ebrahimi, Yunhu Huang, Ali Rashedi, John P. Davis
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lithium ferrite (LiFe) is a promising material for cavity magnonics because its large spin density enables strong coupling between magnons and microwave photons. Its potential for cavity magnomechanics, however, has remained unexplored. Here, we observe magnomechanical interactions in a single-crystal LiFe sphere using coherent microwave feedback to suppress dissipation of the cavity--magnon polariton. In the absence of sufficient feedback, the narrow mechanical response is difficult to resolve against the much broader polariton background. Increasing the feedback gain reduces the polariton linewidth and correspondingly increases the magnomechanical cooperativity, revealing a clear magnomechanically induced transparency feature. In the measurements presented here, the effective upper-polariton linewidth is reduced from [MATH] without feedback to [MATH] in the presence of feedback, while the measured cooperativity increases from [MATH] to [MATH]. These measurements provide, to our knowledge, the first observation of cavity magnomechanics in LiFe and demonstrate coherent feedback as a practical route for accessing weak interactions that would otherwise be obscured by dissipation.
tldr: First observation of cavity magnomechanics in lithium ferrite using coherent microwave feedback to suppress dissipation and enhance cooperativity.
motivation: To explore magnomechanical interactions in lithium ferrite, a material with strong coupling but previously unobserved mechanical response.
method: Used coherent microwave feedback to reduce polariton linewidth and increase magnomechanical cooperativity, revealing a magnomechanically induced transparency feature.
result: Reduced upper-polariton linewidth from [MATH] to [MATH] and increased cooperativity from [MATH] to [MATH].
conclusion: Demonstrates feedback as a practical route to access weak interactions that would otherwise be obscured by dissipation.

By increasing the feedback gain, they reduce the effective upper-polariton linewidth from 3.53 MHz to 5.8 kHz, and correspondingly increase the magnomechanical cooperativity from 1.9×10^-3 to 0.15. title: Affine-Profile Stabilizer Thresholds For Magic In Codeword-Stabilized Quantum Codes
authors: En-Jui Kuo Li-Yi Hsu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Codeword-stabilized quantum codes give a unified graph-state description of stabilizer and nonadditive quantum error-correcting codes. Although each individual CWS word state is stabilizer, coherent superpositions of different word states can be nonstabilizer. We develop a CWS-adapted magic-witness framework that isolates this codeword coherence and converts it into certified lower bounds on robustness of magic. The main result is an exact reduction of the stabilizer threshold of a natural CWS coherence witness to a finite-geometric problem over the classical CWS word set. For general weighted superpositions, the threshold is computed by enumerating affine intersections and affine-quadratic phases. For equal-weight superpositions, the phase optimization collapses, and the threshold is determined entirely by how many CWS words can lie in affine flats of each dimension. Thus a quantum optimization over stabilizer states becomes a classical affine-incidence problem. This reduction yields a fixed-parameter algorithm, an analytic lower bound for an infinite union-stabilizer family, and exact rational certificates for several standard nonadditive CWS examples. The framework also clarifies why exact enumeration fails for large structured families and identifies the remaining task as an affine-intersection problem. The result provides a geometric mechanism by which nonlinear CWS word sets generate certifiable magic.
tldr: This paper develops a framework to certify magic (nonstabilizerness) in codeword-stabilized quantum codes by reducing the stabilizer threshold to a classical affine-intersection problem.
motivation: The paper aims to certify magic in nonadditive quantum codes, which is important for quantum computing, by providing a geometric characterization of when codeword superpositions are nonstabilizer.
method: They introduce a CWS-adapted magic witness that isolates codeword coherence and reduces the computation of stabilizer thresholds to finite-geometric problems over classical CWS word sets, specifically affine intersections and phases.
result: They provide exact reductions yielding fixed-parameter algorithms, analytic lower bounds for infinite families, and exact rational certificates for standard nonadditive CWS examples.
conclusion: The work clarifies the geometric mechanism by which nonlinear CWS word sets generate certifiable magic and identifies open problems in affine-intersection enumeration.

title: Hardware-Aware Fermion-to-Qubit Mappings For Simulating The 2d Hubbard Model On Heavy-Hexagon Quantum Processors
authors: Alessio Esposito, Andrea Giachero, Zolt\`an Zimbor\`as, Leonardo Banchi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated fermionic systems is among the most promising near- term applications of quantum computing, but its practical efficiency depends critically on the choice of fermion-to-qubit mapping and on the connectivity of the underlying hardware. In this work we address this problem in the context of the two-dimensional Hubbard model, simulated on IBM superconducting quantum processors with heavy-hexagon connectivity. We numerically benchmark the Jordan-Wigner, Bravyi-Kitaev, and Bonsai transformations, evaluating their Pauli weight and SWAP overhead across seven heavy-hexagon chips of increasing size. We show that, while the Bravyi-Kitaev mapping initially exhibits a lower Pauli weight, this advantage is eliminated once routing costs are taken into account, confirming the Bonsai mapping as the most hardware-efficient baseline transformation for this architecture. We then use the Bonsai mapping to construct the qubit Hamiltonian of the 2D spinful Fermi-Hubbard model, introducing a simulated annealing algorithm that optimizes the assignment of Majorana strings to lattice sites, reducing the cost function by nearly 50% percent. Finally, we simulate on quantum hardware the time evolution of fermionic states up to 6x6 lattices, confirming the viability of the Bonsai encoding for hardware-aware large-scale two-dimensional simulations.
tldr: This paper benchmarks fermion-to-qubit mappings for the 2D Hubbard model on IBM heavy-hexagon quantum processors and introduces a simulated annealing algorithm to optimize the Bonsai mapping, reducing cost by nearly 50% and enabling simulation of up to 6x6 lattices.
motivation: To enable efficient quantum simulation of strongly correlated fermionic systems like the Hubbard model on near-term quantum hardware, considering hardware connectivity constraints.

title: Certified Decoding Of Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Ragavi Krishnamoorthy, Florian Gerhardt, Johannes Knaute, Thomas Klir, Stefan Raimund Maschek, Erik Schulze, Tomislav Maras, Alexander Dotterweich, Loong Kuan Lee, Christian Bauckhage, Nico Piatkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes reduce the qubit overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation by an order of magnitude, but their decoding is harder than its classical counterpart: because many physical errors are equivalent up to stabilizers, the degenerate maximum-likelihood (ML) decoder must compare the probabilities of entire equivalence classes of errors, that is, partition functions, rather than single errors. The workhorse decoder BP+OSD sidesteps degeneracy heuristically and offers no guarantees. We treat degenerate decoding as probabilistic inference in an undirected graphical model: the probability of each logical class is the partition function of an unconstrained, strictly positive Markov random field over the code's check variables, a construction that generalizes the random-bond Ising mapping of the surface code to arbitrary CSS codes and to spacetime decoding with measurement errors and circuit-level noise. On this model we build two decoders. The first estimates all class partition functions by annealed importance sampling with common random numbers and attaches to every decision a certificate of optimality: a paired bootstrap test, or, composed with constant-factor estimators such as WISH, an exact optimality proof. The second is region-based: the Bethe free energy, whose bias cancels between classes, reproduces exact ML decoding on every tested surface-code instance at millisecond cost, and enlarging the regions to elimination clusters makes exact degenerate ML decoding of the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code feasible. Across surface codes and the bivariate bicycle codes [[72,12,6]] and [[144,12,12]], under code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise, the sampling decoder matches or exceeds BP+OSD while certifying the bulk of its decisions, and the certificate flags exactly the syndromes on which any fast decoder should be distrusted.
tldr: This paper introduces a probabilistic inference framework for degenerate decoding of quantum LDPC codes, enabling certified optimality of decoding decisions.
motivation: Decoding qLDPC codes is challenging due to degeneracy, and existing decoders like BP+OSD lack guarantees, hindering reliable fault-tolerant quantum computation.
method: The authors model degenerate decoding as partition function estimation in a Markov random field over check variables, then propose two decoders: one using annealed importance sampling with certificates, and another using Bethe free energy with elimination clusters for exact decoding.
result: The sampling decoder matches or exceeds BP+OSD on surface codes and bivariate bicycle codes under various noise models, while certifying the majority of decisions and identifying syndromes where fast decoders are unreliable.
conclusion: The provided certified decoding approach significantly improves the reliability and trustworthiness of qLDPC code decoding, advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing.

The paper reformulates degenerate decoding as probabilistic inference in an undirected graphical model, showing that the probability of each logical class is the partition function of a strictly positive Markov random field over the code's check variables. title: High-Fidelity Entangled States In A Connectivity-Four Fluxonium Quantum Processor
authors: J. Schirk, N. Bruckmoser, S. M. Taubenberger, F. Wallner, N. J. Glaser, M. Zetzl, L. Huang, I. Tsitsilin, M. Werninghaus, L. S\"odergren, K. Liegener, C. M. F. Schneider, Stefan Filipp
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central challenge in fluxonium-based quantum processors is the extension of the qubit connectivity to two-dimensional lattices compatible with quantum code-error correction. Here, we present a fluxonium quantum processor that employs lumped-element resonator couplers which realizes, for the first time, a connectivity-four unit cell with suppressed parasitic interactions. We achieve parallel single-qubit gate fidelities exceeding 99.9 % in simultaneous randomized benchmarking experiments, while maintaining residual static ZZ interactions below 1 kHz across all coupled qubit pairs. We implement resonator-induced phase (RIP) gates and benchmark two-qubit gate fidelities exceeding 99 % using interleaved randomized benchmarking. To cancel spectator errors observed in two-qubit operations, we implement a refocused RIP gate, recovering coherent control in the presence of multi-qubit connectivity. Furthermore, we prepare Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states of up to five qubits with a tomographic fidelity of 90 %, verifying multi-qubit entanglement within the unit cell. These results establish the fluxonium-resonator-fluxonium architecture as a viable approach to realizing densely connected fluxonium processors and provide a scalable path toward quantum error-correction-compatible processor architectures.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a fluxonium quantum processor with connectivity-four using resonator couplers, achieving high gate fidelities and preparing GHZ states.
motivation: To extend fluxonium-based processors to 2D lattices for quantum error correction, addressing the challenge of connectivity and parasitic interactions.
method: They use lumped-element resonator couplers to realize a connectivity-four unit cell, implement resonator-induced phase (RIP) gates, and refocused RIP gates to cancel spectator errors.
result: They achieve single-qubit fidelities >99.9%, two-qubit fidelities >99%, and prepare GHZ states of up to five qubits with 90% fidelity.
conclusion: This establishes the fluxonium-resonator-fluxonium architecture as a scalable path for densely connected processors compatible with quantum error correction.

title: Heat Transfer And Torque In Enclosing Cylindrical Configurations With Nonreciprocal Materials
authors: Dhruv Shah, Kiryl Asheichyk, David Gelbwaser-Klimovsky, Noah Graham, Mehran Kardar, Matthias Kr\"uger
abstract: ArXiv:2608.24967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electromagnetic fluctuations can transfer not only energy but also angular momentum, leading to forces, torques, heat currents, and friction in out-of-equilibrium setups. In enclosing configurations, we show that if at least one of two objects is rotationally symmetric, the torque is bounded by heat transfer, since both arise from photon transfers with angular momentum [MATH] and energy [MATH]. With only one object assumed to be rotationally symmetric, it may be possible to obtain a nonzero torque with reciprocal media, but nonreciprocal media are required to break the symmetry between [MATH] and [MATH] and produce a nonzero torque if both objects are rotationally symmetric. We then specialize to concentric cylinders with a nonreciprocal dielectric response and use Rytov fluctuational electrodynamics to express heat transfer and torque in terms of an angular-momentum-resolved flux density, [MATH]. We also analyze the conditions for stable levitation of the inner cylinder using the proximity force approximation, in the process obtaining a new analytic formula for the normal Casimir force between dilute plates at different temperatures. Finally, to find the extracted work in a contactless engine setup, we compute the fluctuation-induced friction for a slowly rotating inner cylinder, and we find a bound between torque, friction, and heat transfer. Due to this bound, the efficiency of the heat engine remains bounded by the Carnot limit.
tldr: This paper studies heat transfer, torque, and friction in cylindrical configurations with nonreciprocal materials, deriving bounds that limit the efficiency of contactless heat engines to the Carnot limit.

method: Uses Rytov fluctuational electrodynamics to express heat transfer and torque via an angular-momentum-resolved flux density, and applies the proximity force approximation for the normal Casimir force between dilute plates.
result: Establishes that torque is bounded by heat transfer when at least one object is rotationally symmetric, and nonreciprocal media are needed for nonzero torque when both are symmetric; derives bounds between torque, friction, and heat transfer.
conclusion: The efficiency of a contactless heat engine in this configuration is bounded by the Carnot limit, and stable levitation conditions are analyzed.

title: Quantum Skyrmion Parallelism Via Metasurface-tailored High-dimensional Entanglement
authors: Pedro Ornelas, Ramona Bedford, Fazilah Nothlawala, Chi Li, Haoyi Yu, Isaac Nape, Stefan A. Maier, Haoran Ren, Andrew Forbes
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum skyrmions are topological structures that have garnered significant interest due to their demonstrated robustness and versatility across diverse optical platforms. However, existing approaches for their generation are limited to producing pre-determined two dimensional qubit states with a single topology. Here we create multi-dimensional topological states by introducing a non-local interaction between high-dimensional photonic entanglement and a metasurface, where the topological transformation induced by the metasurface is made non-deterministic by the probabilistic nature of the interfacing entangled state. Within this framework, we demonstrate that individual quantum states can host multiple co-existing topologies that are only revealed upon measurement, allowing for their parallel transport within distinct spatial mode channels. We confirm this by revealing the rich topological landscape within our modified Hilbert space while controlling the desired output topology by orbital angular momentum (OAM) projections on one of the entangled photons, producing multiple non-local polarization-OAM entangled states characterized by distinct topological classes, all from a single metasurface device. Our results reveal new capability when structured high-dimensional entanglement is interfaced with structured matter capable of coupling photonic degrees of freedom, establishing a new pathway for the compact generation of complex quantum states.

title: A Unified Framework For Operator Backpropagation And Observable Measurement In Quantum Computing
authors: Ji Liu Kevin Dougherty
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoherence imposes severe limits on quantum circuit depth, motivating methods to reduce circuit depth. Operator backpropagation has recently been proposed as a way to lower circuit depth by classically backpropagating observables through subcircuits. While it lowers the circuit depth, it also significantly increases the number of backpropagated observables that must be measured. This calls for an efficient measurement protocol tailored to these backpropagated observables. Moreover, errors arise both during the backpropagation procedure and during measurement, and they accumulate in the final computation. No prior work has examined how to integrate operator backpropagation with advanced measurement protocols, and how to jointly optimize the combined process. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive framework to determine the appropriate measurement protocol to achieve a desired level of accuracy with the fewest number of measurements based on the number of qubit-wise commuting (QWC) groups formed from operator backpropagation. We analyze and categorize the primary sources of error that arise through our workflow, including error incurred from the backpropagation algorithm, truncation error, and shot noise variation. We also examine truncation strategies to reduce the number of backpropagated observables by characterizing the structure of the set of backpropagated observables.
tldr: The paper presents a unified framework for operator backpropagation in quantum circuits that optimizes measurement protocols to minimize the number of measurements while achieving target accuracy and analyzing error sources.
motivation: Decoherence limits quantum circuit depth, and operator backpropagation reduces depth but increases the number of observables to measure, necessitating efficient measurement protocols and error analysis.
method: The framework determines optimal measurement protocols based on qubit-wise commuting (QWC) groups, categorizes errors (backpropagation, truncation, shot noise), and develops truncation strategies to reduce the number of backpropagated observables.
result: It provides a systematic approach to select measurement protocols and analyze errors, achieving desired accuracy with fewer measurements.
conclusion: The framework enables joint optimization of backpropagation and measurement, improving the efficiency of quantum computations under decoherence.

title: No Free Compression In Quantum Relaxations For Optimization
authors: Stuart Hadfield
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Qubit-efficient quantum relaxations compress classical decision variables into expectation values on substantially fewer qubits. We ask what resource tradeoffs this compression entails for quantum optimization. We define the universal margin as the smallest correlator magnitude that can be guaranteed with prescribed signs for every target sign assignment. We show that it is exactly [MATH], whereas uniformly random sign assignments retain [MATH] target-specific margins. The stronger [MATH] worst-case scaling is Majorana-specific. Moreover, arbitrary density operators and fermionic Gaussian states generate the same quadratic-Majorana covariance body, so non-Gaussian state resources cannot enlarge this two-point relaxation. Beyond Majoranas, standard quantum random access code bounds provide general information-theoretic baselines. For any fixed family of [MATH] designated binary observables on [MATH] qubits, the universal margin is at most [MATH], while arbitrary random access decoding from [MATH] copies with constant success probability above [MATH] requires [MATH]. For a fixed Pauli correlation encoding required to work uniformly over all targets, maintaining a fixed nonzero decoded magnitude under smooth sign decoding therefore requires a rescaling parameter that grows as the available margin shrinks. Thus, while providing substantial qubit savings, compression can shift cost into restricted expectation value geometry, smaller expectation value magnitudes, or more demanding information recovery rather than eliminate it.

They define the 'universal margin' as the smallest correlator magnitude that can be guaranteed for any target sign assignment, and prove that for this encoding the universal margin is exactly Δ_Maj(n) = tan(π/(4n)) = Θ(1/n). In contrast, for uniformly random sign assignments, the typical margin is Θ(1/√n), indicating that worst-case assignments are significantly harder. The paper also shows that the set of achievable covariance matrices for quadratic-Majorana encodings is identical for arbitrary density operators and fermionic Gaussian states, implying that non-Gaussian states do not enlarge the relaxation. Beyond Majoranas, the authors derive general information-theoretic bounds using quantum random access codes: for any fixed family of m binary observables on n qubits, the universal margin is at most √(2 ln 2 · n/m), and decoding from N copies with constant success probability above 1/2 requires nN = Ω(m). These results highlight that while qubit-efficient encodings save qubits, they impose constraints on expectation value magnitudes and information recovery.

title: Superextensive Learning In Quantum Reservoirs At The Onset Of Information Scrambling
authors: Francesco Campaioli Jonas Freiheit
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The idea that information processing is optimised near the boundary between order and chaos has emerged as a recurring principle across neuroscience, complex systems, and machine learning. Here we test this hypothesis in quantum many-body systems, numerically simulating two-dimensional Ising networks of up to [MATH] spins, operated as quantum reservoirs for time-series forecasting. Using out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs), we locate the onset of information scrambling as the input strength is swept, separating regimes where information is frozen and scrambled across the whole reservoir state. We show that prediction precision peaks at the onset of scrambling, along with the number of computational-basis states that the reservoir actively populates. We then show that prediction precision grows as a power law [MATH] in the reservoir size, superextensively [MATH] at the onset of scrambling and only sublinearly [MATH] in either neighbouring regime. Finally, we show that scrambling enhances the nonlinear components of the reservoir memory while reducing its linear capacity. At the onset, the total memory capacity grows superextensively, provided that the necessary ``forgetting'' mechanism is supplied by a collective relaxation channel. These results consolidate the role of information scrambling in learning systems, turning it from an operating point into a scaling law for the performance of quantum reservoirs.

motivation: The hypothesis that information processing is optimized near the boundary between order and chaos is tested in quantum many-body systems, aiming to connect fundamental physics with machine learning performance.
method: Numerically simulate two-dimensional Ising networks as quantum reservoirs for time-series forecasting, using out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) to identify the onset of information scrambling as input strength is varied, and analyze prediction precision and memory capacities.
result: Prediction precision peaks at the onset of scrambling, growing superextensively with reservoir size, while memory capacity also grows superextensively when a collective relaxation channel provides the necessary forgetting mechanism; scrambling enhances nonlinear memory but reduces linear capacity.
conclusion: Information scrambling acts as a key operating point for quantum reservoirs, turning the onset of chaos into a scaling law that guides the design of efficient learning systems.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computing: real-time decoding at scale.
The demonstration on a single CPU makes the solution practical and accessible, avoiding the need for specialized hardware.
The benchmarking on realistic workloads (up to 408 qubits, one million T gates) provides strong evidence of scalability.
The quantitative analysis of decoding overhead as a function of error rate gives clear performance metrics.
limitations: The paper focuses on a specific trapped-ion architecture, and the results may not directly generalize to other qubit modalities (e.g., superconducting or photonic).
The abstract does not specify the decoding algorithm used, nor does it provide absolute decoding times or a breakdown of the pipeline's latency, which would be useful for a deeper understanding.
The study assumes a fixed cycle time (1-5 ms) and may not account for variations in syndrome extraction or other architectural details that could affect decoding time.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computing, which are core topics in quantum physics. The demonstration of real-time decoding at MegaQuOp scale addresses a key challenge in scaling quantum computers, and the methodology (simulation of trapped-ion architectures) aligns with research on quantum hardware and error correction. The results provide insights into the practical feasibility of fault-tolerant quantum computation, which is of interest to researchers working on quantum algorithms, quantum information theory, and experimental quantum computing.

The use of a single CPU is a notable achievement, and the benchmarking on realistic workloads provides strong evidence of practicality. The paper is well-written and the results are convincing, though the lack of algorithmic details and absolute timing data is a minor drawback. Overall, this is a high-quality contribution that will likely influence the design of future quantum computing systems and decoding strategies.

title: Comment On 'Supervised Quantum Machine Learning Models Are Kernel Methods'
authors: Rajiv Krishnakumar
abstract: ArXiv:2608.24923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We identify a few small errors in the proof of Theorem 1 in M. Schuld, 'Supervised quantum machine learning models are kernel methods' (arXiv:2101.11020v2), Appendix A. These do not affect the validity of the theorem, but do matter if one wants to use the appendix to explicitly compute the Fourier coefficients of a quantum kernel. We give the corrected derivation, and additionally show that the paper's worked cosine-kernel example contains a second, unrelated error that happens to cancel the first, thereby coincidentally yielding the correct result.
tldr: This comment corrects errors in the proof of Theorem 1 from Schuld's paper on supervised quantum machine learning models being kernel methods, providing a corrected derivation and identifying a coincidental error cancellation in the cosine kernel example.
motivation: To ensure the mathematical correctness of the theoretical foundation that supervised quantum machine learning models can be represented as kernel methods, which is important for explicit computation of quantum kernel coefficients.
method: The author re-derives the Fourier coefficients of a quantum kernel, fixing the errors in the original Appendix A derivation and also pinpointing an unrelated error that cancels the first, yielding the correct result.
result: The corrected derivation yields the correct Fourier coefficients, and the worked example still produces the expected outcome due to the cancellation of errors.
conclusion: The original theorem remains valid, but the corrected derivations are necessary for practical use of the appendix to compute quantum kernel coefficients explicitly.

title: High-density Optical Quantum Sensors With Pulsed Probe Read-out For Correlated Spin-Noise Reduction
authors: Young Jin Kim Igor Savukov
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical quantum sensors based on alkali-metal atoms enable highly sensitive magnetic-field measurements at room temperature. Their ultimate performance is limited by intrinsic spin noise once technical noise sources are sufficiently suppressed. Reducing and characterizing this noise is therefore essential for improving sensor sensitivity and for investigating quantum-enhanced sensing protocols. Here we investigate correlated spin fluctuations in a radio-frequency optical quantum sensor based on a high-density potassium vapor cell using a pulsed probe readout scheme. The system employs orthogonal pump and probe laser beams, while a static magnetic field defines the sensing frequency and synchronizes the probe pulses with the spin precession. To detect weak spin correlations, we implement a measurement protocol that combines periodic probing, phase cycling, and window-shifted acquisition. Phase cycling suppresses reproducible probe-induced coherent transients, while subtraction of temporally correlated signals acquired within the spin-relaxation time reduces the measured spin-noise level. The observed noise reduction is consistent with temporal spin correlations, including those expected in spin-squeezing protocols, although the present measurements do not uniquely distinguish this interpretation from other correlated-noise mechanisms. The demonstrated measurement protocol provides a practical route toward operating warm-vapor optical quantum sensors closer to their fundamental spin-noise limit and may benefit radio-frequency magnetometry and sensing of weak coherent signals, including emerging dark-matter detection schemes.
tldr: This paper experimentally investigates correlated spin noise in a high-density potassium vapor cell using a pulsed probe readout scheme to reduce spin noise and improve optical quantum sensor sensitivity.
motivation: Optical quantum sensors based on alkali-metal atoms are limited by intrinsic spin noise; reducing this noise is essential for improving sensitivity and enabling quantum-enhanced sensing protocols.
method: The system uses orthogonal pump and probe beams with a pulsed probe readout, combined with phase cycling and window-shifted acquisition to suppress coherent transients and reduce spin-noise levels.
result: Observed noise reduction is consistent with temporal spin correlations, though not uniquely distinguishable from other correlated-noise mechanisms.
conclusion: The demonstrated protocol provides a practical route toward operating warm-vapor optical quantum sensors closer to their fundamental spin-noise limit, benefiting radio-frequency magnetometry and weak-signal sensing.

title: Nonlocal Thermal Noise In Electrically Coupled Conductors: A Microscopic Two-dimensional Study
authors: Jorge Berger
abstract: ArXiv:2608.24980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Johnson-Nyquist theory is commonly implemented by representing a conductor as a collection of independent local thermal-noise sources whose strength is determined by the local temperature. Whether this local-noise representation remains valid for electrically coupled conductors maintained at different temperatures has received comparatively little attention. We investigate this question by means of microscopic two-dimensional simulations of interacting charge carriers in conducting wires capacitively coupled. The model reproduces Ohm's law, the equilibrium Johnson noise, and vanishing correlations between detached wire segments when both wires are at the same temperature. However, when the wires are held at different temperatures, finite correlations develop between the electromotive forces generated in distant segments, leading to systematic deviations of the Johnson temperature inferred from the local-noise picture. The effect persists although the microscopic particle interactions are short-ranged and the two wires interact only through the capacitive coupling. These results suggest that the independent-local-source representation of thermal noise may not remain valid in electrically coupled nonequilibrium conductors.
tldr: This paper investigates whether the local noise source representation in Johnson-Nyquist theory remains valid for coupled conductors at different temperatures, finding that correlations emerge and cause deviations.
motivation: The standard Johnson-Nyquist theory assumes independent local thermal noise sources. The validity of this assumption for non-equilibrium coupled conductors is questioned.
method: The authors use microscopic two-dimensional simulations of interacting charge carriers in capacitively coupled wires.
result: At equal temperatures, the model matches Ohm's law and equilibrium noise, but at different temperatures, finite correlations develop between distant electromotive forces, leading to systematic deviations in the inferred Johnson temperature.
conclusion: The independent-local-source representation of thermal noise may fail in coupled non-equilibrium conductors.

title: First-Principles Prediction Of Nonlinear Optical Response In $\text{TiO}_2$ For High-Power Dielectric Mirror Applications
authors: Koya Shimaoka, Yusuke Kondo, Kazunori Shibata, Mitsuharu Uemoto
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dielectric multilayer mirrors are essential components in optical experiments using high-power lasers, where titanium dioxide ([MATH]) is widely employed as a high-refractive-index dielectric material. In this study, we investigate the nonlinear optical response of [MATH] under intense ultrashort laser pulses using real-time first-principles electron-dynamics simulations based on time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT). We reveal intensity-dependent absorption driven by multiphoton excitation and optically excited free carriers, and simulate the resulting electron--light coupled dynamics in [MATH] nanofilms using a multiscale Maxwell--TDDFT framework. Direct evaluation of the reflected and transmitted fields shows reduced reflectance at high intensities ([MATH]), demonstrating a pronounced nonlinear optical response. Furthermore, the optical response properties are compared among various stable and metastable crystalline phases of [MATH]---rutile, anatase, brookite, [MATH]-II, and [MATH]-B---as well as an amorphous supercell model. These results provide microscopic insight into intensity-dependent optical degradation in [MATH]-based dielectric optical components exposed to intense femtosecond laser fields.
tldr: This paper uses first-principles TDDFT simulations to study nonlinear optical response in TiO2 for high-power dielectric mirror applications, revealing intensity-dependent absorption and reflectance reduction.
motivation: Dielectric multilayer mirrors are essential for high-power lasers, and TiO2 is a key material; understanding its nonlinear optical response under intense ultrashort pulses is crucial for predicting performance limitations.
method: The authors employ real-time time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) electron-dynamics simulations and a multiscale Maxwell-TDDFT framework to simulate electron-light coupled dynamics in TiO2 nanofilms.
result: They find reduced reflectance at high intensities due to multiphoton excitation and free-carrier absorption, and compare optical response across different TiO2 phases (rutile, anatase, brookite, etc.) and amorphous models.
conclusion: The results provide microscopic insight into intensity-dependent optical degradation in TiO2-based dielectric components, which is important for high-power laser applications.

title: Generalized Efficient Quantum Circuit Implementation Of Discrete-Time Quantum Walks On Cayley Graphs
authors: Seoyoon Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a generalized and efficient quantum circuit framework for implementing discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs) on Cayley graphs of arbitrary dimension. Building on the Boundary QFT scheme of Razzoli et al., we introduce a systematic multi-stage decomposition of the shift operator for 1D Cayley graphs across three classes of generating sets: inverse-closed without involutions, inverse-closed with an involution, and non-inverse-closed. The decomposition hierarchically factorizes the QFT-diagonalized shift operator into structured block components, progressively reducing the control degree of the required rotation gates and replacing high-degree multi-qubit controlled operations with collections of lower-degree equivalents. We extend this construction to [MATH]-dimensional torus graphs and provide explicit circuit implementations for an 8-Cayley graph and a [MATH] torus graph as concrete illustrations. Gate complexity analysis using the linear CNOT scaling of Rosa et al. demonstrates that the decomposed implementation achieves a substantial reduction in upper-bound CNOT cost relative to the naive implementation within the regime [MATH] for inverse-closed graphs and [MATH] for non-inverse-closed graphs, where [MATH] denotes the degree of the generating set. Benchmarking further reveals that this efficiency gain is largely insensitive to the system size [MATH], identifying [MATH] as the dominant resource parameter for the shift operator. These results provide a scalable and hardware-conscious pathway toward practical DTQW implementations on near-term quantum devices.
tldr: This paper presents a generalized efficient quantum circuit framework for discrete-time quantum walks on Cayley graphs, focusing on gate complexity reduction for near-term devices.
motivation: To enable scalable and practical implementation of quantum walks on near-term quantum hardware by reducing circuit resource requirements.
method: Builds on the Boundary QFT scheme, introduces a multi-stage decomposition of the shift operator for various generating sets, and extends the construction to higher-dimensional torus graphs with explicit circuit examples and gate complexity analysis.
result: The decomposed implementation achieves a substantial reduction in CNOT cost compared to naive implementations, with efficiency largely insensitive to system size but dependent on the degree of the generating set.
conclusion: The proposed framework offers a scalable and hardware-conscious pathway for practical DTQW implementations on near-term quantum devices.

title: The Temperature-dependent non-Abelian Gauge Potential
authors: Zheng-Chuan Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study shows that the usual time evolution operator can act as a U(1) gauge transformation on the initial wavefuntion. When considering the spin freedom in the system, the time evolution operator corresponds to a non-Abelian SU(2) gauge transformation for spin-1/2 particles and a SU(3) gauge transformation for spin-1 particles. If we adopt the adiabatic approximation in the magnetization dynamics of a ferromagnetic system driven by a spin-polarized current, a temperature-dependent non-Abelian thermal gauge potential will appear. We can employ a temperature-dependent Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) equation to describe the magnetization dynamics in the semi-classical limit, a linear approximated solution for this equation is given analytically.
tldr: 该论文研究温度依赖的非阿贝尔规范势，及其在铁磁系统磁化动力学中的应用。
motivation: 探索时间演化算符的规范变换性质，并考虑温度影响下的非阿贝尔规范势。
method: 通过绝热近似推导温度依赖的规范势，并建立半经典极限下的LLG方程。
result: 得到温度依赖的LLG方程及其线性近似解析解。
conclusion: 揭示了温度对非阿贝尔规范势的影响，为磁化动力学提供理论框架。

title: Free-Energy Asymptotics Of The Two-Dimensional Quantum Heisenberg Ferromagnet
authors: Andreas Klippel
abstract: ArXiv:2608.25506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the leading low-temperature free-energy asymptotics of the nearest-neighbour quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet on [MATH]. For every fixed [MATH], the free energy per site satisfies \[ \lim_{\beta\to\infty}\beta^2S f_2(\beta,S)=-{24}. \] This formula was predicted by Takahashi's modified spin-wave theory [15]. Napi\'orkowski and Seiringer proved the corresponding upper bound but left the matching lower bound in two dimensions open [13], a gap later highlighted again by Seiringer [14]. We prove this missing bound through a new comparison between the magnon exclusion dynamics and free bosons, based on extending wave functions to collision configurations with controlled kinetic cost.
tldr: Proves the leading low-temperature free-energy asymptotics of the 2D quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet, confirming Takahashi's modified spin-wave theory prediction.
motivation: To resolve the missing lower bound in two dimensions, a gap highlighted by Napiórkowski and Seiringer.
method: Extends wave functions to collision configurations with controlled kinetic cost, enabling a comparison between magnon exclusion dynamics and free bosons.
result: Demonstrates that the free energy per site satisfies the expected limit as β→∞.
conclusion: Confirms the theoretical prediction and completes the proof of the free-energy asymptotic formula in 2D.
